scenes.headline: asyncio for Concurrent Ingestion
scenes.subtitle: Thousands of I/O tasks on one thread
scenes.narration: asyncio lets a single thread juggle thousands of network calls at once, making it the ideal tool for high-throughput ingestion from many APIs, streams, or endpoints.

scenes.headline: Core concepts
items: async def defines a coroutine that can pause and resume
await yields control back to the event loop during I/O
The event loop schedules ready coroutines on one thread
scenes.narration: An async def function is a coroutine, a special function that can suspend itself partway through and be resumed later. The await keyword marks a point where the coroutine hands control back to the event loop while it waits on I/O. The event loop is the conductor: it keeps a single thread busy by running whichever coroutine is ready, so idle waiting is never wasted.

scenes.headline: asyncio vs threads for I/O
scenes.narration: Both models overlap I/O waits, but they scale differently. asyncio runs everything cooperatively on one thread, so tasks are nearly free and you can launch tens of thousands, provided your libraries are async-aware. Threads work with any blocking library out of the box, but each carries real memory overhead and the operating system limits how many you can practically run. Reach for asyncio at high concurrency, and threads when you must call a synchronous library.

scenes.headline: Concurrent fetches with gather
scenes.code:
import asyncio
import aiohttp

async def fetch(session, url):
    async with session.get(url) as resp:
        return await resp.json()

async def main(urls):
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        tasks = [fetch(session, u) for u in urls]
        return await asyncio.gather(*tasks)

results = asyncio.run(main(url_list))
scenes.narration: Here aiohttp provides an async HTTP client whose requests can be awaited. The main coroutine builds a list of fetch tasks without running them yet, then asyncio.gather launches them all and waits for every result together. Because each fetch releases control during its network wait, all of the requests overlap on one thread, and asyncio.run drives the whole thing from ordinary synchronous code.

scenes.headline: Bounding concurrency with a Semaphore
scenes.code:
import asyncio

sem = asyncio.Semaphore(20)

async def fetch_limited(session, url):
    async with sem:
        async with session.get(url) as resp:
            return await resp.json()
scenes.narration: Firing off ten thousand requests at once will overwhelm a server or trip its rate limits, so you almost always cap concurrency. An asyncio.Semaphore initialized to twenty permits only that many coroutines inside the guarded block at a time, forcing the rest to wait their turn. This simple pattern turns unbounded parallelism into a well-behaved, throttled ingestion pipeline.

scenes.headline: Pitfalls to avoid
items: A blocking call freezes the entire event loop
Always await coroutines, or they never run
scenes.narration: The gravest asyncio mistake is calling blocking code, since a single synchronous request or heavy computation stalls the one thread and every other task with it. When you must use blocking libraries, push them onto a thread pool via run_in_executor. And remember that a coroutine does nothing until awaited, so a forgotten await is a silent bug where the work simply never happens.

scenes.text: asyncio scales I/O-bound ingestion massively on one thread — just never block the loop and always bound your concurrency.
scenes.narration: For ingesting from many endpoints at once, asyncio delivers enormous concurrency on a single thread. Keep the loop unblocked and cap your parallelism, and it becomes a rock-solid foundation for high-throughput pipelines.
